{"voice_profile":"Brisk, light-comic thriller voice. Most of the story moves through quick dialogue, broken by dashes and suspense ellipses, with italics for emphasis. The narrator adds dry, ironic asides ("using the words that have created many unnecessary panics"; "Julius’s narrative style, if not strictly accurate, was picturesque!"). Each character has a strong verbal tag. Julius speaks in American slang and tall talk ("Little Willie," "Sure thing," "I guess"). Tuppence is pert and bossy. Tommy is curt and understated. Sir James speaks in measured, lawyerly cadence. Kramenin is shrill and hissing. Melodrama is played straight and then punctured by a joke.","book_context":"The plot runs on bluff, impersonation and withheld knowledge. Tuppence's 'Jane Finn' bluff, Tommy's bargain in Soho, and Jane's feigned amnesia all mirror Mr. Brown's own mask. Brown is the 'nonentity' with an ordinary face, hidden in a crowd. All through the book Sir James drops hints and Julius keeps secrets (the safe), so the reader is set to suspect each in turn. Chapters XXIV–XXVI hold the double reveal in strict order. XXIV: Julius rescues the girls, and Tommy turns the gun on him for reasons left unexplained. XXV: Jane's story, then Sir James accuses 'Julius.' XXVI: Sir James unmasks himself and dies. XXVII then explains everything at the Savoy, through Tommy's account and Brown's diary. Setups to keep intact: the 'Twopence' note, the Marguerite/Faust picture, the peep-hole, Little Willie, the brandy, the photograph in the safe, the recess curtain, the Argentine note, and Tommy's uncle and Tuppence's father.","chapters":[{"id":"025","verbatim":[{"paragraph":28,"text":"“Hands up--or I shoot!”","purpose":"Abrupt tonal switch from drawl to threat; the turning point of the scene."},{"paragraph":52,"text":"I did not know it until afterwards.
